question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer, Investment Manager of Chakra Growth Fund (Cat II AIF), has identified that the appointed independent valuer is the wholly-owned subsidiary of the parent group that also sponsors the AIF. The valuer has submitted a mark-up of 40% on a key investee that is due for IPO exit in 6 months. As Manager, what is the most appropriate course of action?

answer.text: Accept the valuation since the valuer is independent in function, regardless of ownership

Replace the valuer with one that is NOT an associate of the sponsor/manager/trustee (as required by SEBI eligibility) and re-do the valuation, disclosing the deviation to investors if NAV moves by more than 20% quarter-on-quarter
Ignore the conflict since the mark-up is justified by imminent IPO
Reduce the mark-up unilaterally by 50% and retain the valuer

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 14.14, the independent valuer 'shall NOT be an associate of manager or sponsor or trustee of the AIF'. A subsidiary of the sponsor's parent is an associate under any reasonable reading. The correct action is to replace the valuer, re-value, and disclose any deviation under the 20%/33% rule. The Trap: Option A ignores associate-rule. Option C conflates IPO-imminent with conflict-cleansing. Option D (unilateral reduction) is manager-side valuation manipulation — itself a violation. Cross-Exam Context: III-A (Compliance) covers conflict-of-interest; XIX-C tests the manager's operational fix: rotate out the conflicted valuer, document the rationale, re-disclose to LPs. Manager's Pro-Tip: Build valuer rotation into your PPM: no single valuer beyond 3 consecutive financial years, no associate-of-sponsor ever. This defensively handles the Sept-2024 circular and survives any future tightening of SEBI independence norms.
